contentObjective: I can plot and identify points on the coordinate plane using ordered pairs.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Name the Treasure Route Shape
revealWordProblem.text: Captain Vega's three waypoints are at (2, 1), (5, 4), and (8, 1). Plot the three points and connect them in order. What shape does the treasure route make, and what are the coordinates of its three vertices?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The three points form a triangle. Its vertices are (2, 1), (5, 4), and (8, 1).

mission.title: Captain Vega's Coordinates
mission.story: You are the navigator on Captain Vega's expedition. Instead of 'X marks the spot,' she hid the treasure route as ordered pairs scrawled across the first quadrant of her chart, using only positive coordinates. Plot every point in the right order and the lost cove treasure is yours.
mission.objective: Plot ordered pairs accurately on the coordinate plane to trace the treasure route.

scenes.name: Course Plotting

finale.title: Treasure Recovered!

launch.narrative: Captain Vega left a treasure map, but instead of an 'X marks the spot,' she hid the directions as ordered pairs! To find the treasure, you need to plot each point on the coordinate plane and connect them in order. The first clue says: Start at (2, 1), then go to (5, 4), then (8, 1).

conceptIntro.heading: How do you plot a point on the coordinate plane?
conceptIntro.intro: An ordered pair (x, y) is two numbers that tell you exactly where a point goes. The first number moves you right or left. The second number moves you up or down.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Always start at the origin (0, 0), move right/left first, then up/down.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot the point (5, 4). The 5 is the x-coordinate, and the 4 is the y-coordinate.
I start at the origin, which is (0, 0).
First I move 5 units to the right along the x-axis.
Then I move 4 units up. I place my dot. That is the point (5, 4).

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's plot (2, 1). Where do we start? At the origin (0, 0).
How far do we move right? The first number is 2, so we move 2 right.
How far do we move up? The second number is 1, so we move 1 up and place the dot.

youDo.title: Now it's your turn
lines: In the explore, plot Captain Vega's waypoints (2, 1), (5, 4), and (8, 1) to trace the treasure route.

explore.instructions: Plot Captain Vega's treasure map points and connect them to reveal the path!
explore.label: Plot the three treasure map waypoints.

discourse.prompt: You plotted a triangle. How did the ordered pairs tell you exactly where to place each point?
discourse.sentenceFrame: The first number in the ordered pair tells me ___ and the second number tells me ___. The point (5, 4) means ___.

approaching.stem: Which ordered pair names a point 3 units right and 7 units up from the origin?
approaching.explanation: The first coordinate is horizontal (right 3), the second is vertical (up 7). So (3, 7).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
hints: Re-read the moves: 3 units right, then 7 units up. Which move comes first in an ordered pair?
An ordered pair is (x, y): x is the right/left distance, y is the up/down distance. Match each move to its slot.
Start at the origin and go right 3 — that 3 is the x, the first number. Now decide where the 'up 7' goes.

approaching.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?
approaching.explanation: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis cross, at (0, 0).
choiceFeedback: The origin is where both axes cross, where both values are zero.
Both coordinates at the origin are 0 — not mixed with 1.
Check both the x and y values at the origin.
hints: The origin is the exact spot where the x-axis and y-axis cross. Picture that crossing point.
Ask: how far right have you moved at the origin? How far up? Those two distances are the coordinates.
At the crossing point you haven't moved right at all, so x = 0. Now figure out the y-value the same way.

approaching.stem: A point is at (6, 2). What does the 6 tell you?
approaching.explanation: The first number (x-coordinate) tells you horizontal movement. 6 means go right 6 units from the origin.
choiceFeedback: The first number controls horizontal movement—check which number moves you up.
With a positive first number, you move right—not left.
Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: In (6, 2), the 6 is the FIRST number. First and second positions have different jobs.
First number = x = horizontal (right/left). Second number = y = vertical (up/down). Positive means right or up.
The 6 sits in the x spot and it's positive, so it describes a horizontal move. Which direction is positive x?

approaching.label: Put these steps in order for plotting the point (4, 5).
items: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis
Move 5 units up from that spot
Place a dot at the point (4, 5)
correctOrder: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis
Move 5 units up from that spot
Place a dot at the point (4, 5)
approaching.hint: Start with the first step: where do you always begin when plotting?
hints: Every plotting routine begins at the same home spot before any moving happens.
Think: start point, then horizontal move, then vertical move, then mark the dot. Order the cards to tell that story.
Place 'Start at the origin (0, 0)' first. Then ask: does the 4 (x) move or the 5 (y) move come next?

approaching.label: Match each ordered pair to its description.
approaching.hint: Try the first step of the solution process.
hints: Each pair is (x, y): first number = right, second = up. A 0 means you don't move in that direction.
Translate each pair into moves, like (4, 2) = right 4, up 2. Pairs with a 0 in them land ON an axis.
Try (3, 0): right 3, up 0 — you never leave the x-axis. Use that same test on (0, 4) and the rest.

approaching.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Move
workedExample.work: Move up 3, then move right 5, and place the dot.

approaching.correctWork: The student swapped the directions. For (3, 5) you move RIGHT 3 first (the x-coordinate), then UP 5 (the y-coordinate). The dot belongs at right 3, up 5.
hints: In an ordered pair (x, y), which number tells you to move right — the first or the second?
Move right with the first number (3), then up with the second number (5).

onLevel.label: Plot these points to reveal a hidden shape: (1, 1), (1, 5), (6, 5), (6, 1)
onLevel.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Each pair is (x, y). For point A(1, 1) both moves are just 1 unit.
For every point: start at (0, 0), slide right x units along the bottom, then climb up y units.
Plot A first: right 1, up 1. Then B(1, 5): same x, so it sits straight above A — count up to 5.

onLevel.label: Match each point to its quadrant or axis.
onLevel.hint: Try the first step of the solution process.
hints: Check the SIGNS of each coordinate: + or - for x and y decide the quadrant. A 0 means the point sits on an axis.
Quadrants go counterclockwise: I is (+, +), II is (-, +), III is (-, -), IV is (+, -). A 0 puts you on an axis instead.
Take (3, 2): both signs positive, so top-right — Quadrant I. Now check the signs of (-4, 5) the same way.

onLevel.instructions: Complete the table. Write the ordered pair for each description.
onLevel.hint: Complete each row by converting the description to (x, y) form.
hints: 'Right' tells you the x (first number); 'Up' tells you the y (second number).
Write each row as (right amount, up amount). If a move is 0, put 0 in that slot — don't skip it.
Start with row 1: 'Right 7' gives the first number of the pair. Now find which word gives the second number.

onLevel.label: Sort these ordered pairs by their x-coordinate from smallest to largest.
onLevel.hint: Start with the first step: where do you always begin when plotting?
hints: You're sorting by the FIRST number in each pair only — ignore the second number completely.
Underline each x: 5, 1, 3, 0, 7. Then arrange the pairs so those underlined numbers go smallest to largest.
The smallest x here is 0, so (0, 4) goes first — even though its 4 is big. Now find the next-smallest x.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Ordered pair
workedExample.work: Name the quadrant of the point (-2, 6).

workedExample.label: Name the quadrant
workedExample.work: Negative numbers are at the bottom, so the point is in Quadrant III.

onLevel.correctWork: A negative x and a positive y land in the top-left region, which is Quadrant II — not Quadrant III. Quadrant III is where BOTH coordinates are negative (-x, -y).
hints: Quadrant II is (-x, +y) top-left; Quadrant III is (-x, -y) bottom-left. Which one has a positive y?
The point (-2, 6) has a positive y (6), so it is above the x-axis — that is Quadrant II.

extending.title: Find the Plotting Error
extending.correctWork: x-coordinate = horizontal (right 4), NOT vertical. The student swapped x and y directions.
hints: In an ordered pair (x, y), which direction does x go — horizontal or vertical?
x is always horizontal (left/right) first. y is vertical (up/down) second. The student went up first.

extending.prompt: A student says that (3, 5) and (5, 3) are the same point because they use the same numbers. Is the student correct? Explain why or why not, and describe where each point is located on the coordinate plane.
extending.sentenceFrame: The student is ___ because (3, 5) means ___ while (5, 3) means ___. The ORDER matters because ___.
extending.hint: Compare what each coordinate pair tells you about horizontal and vertical moves.
hints: Both pairs use 3 and 5, but look at which number sits in the x (first) spot in each pair.
Describe each point's moves separately: (3, 5) = right ?, up ?; (5, 3) = right ?, up ?. Compare the two paths.
First step: for (3, 5), go right 3 and up 5. Now do (5, 3)'s moves and check whether you land on the same dot.

extending.label: Plot the points (2, 3), (2, 7), (6, 7), (6, 3). Connect them. Name the shape and find its perimeter using the coordinates.
extending.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Plot all 4 points first. Notice A and B share x = 2, and B and C share y = 7 — that makes straight sides.
Count side lengths on the grid, or subtract coordinates: same-x sides use the y-values, same-y sides use the x-values.
Side AB runs from (2, 3) to (2, 7): count 7 − 3 units. Find the other side lengths, then add all four.

workedExample.label: Plot the point
workedExample.work: Move right 5, then up 2, and place the dot at (5, 2).

optional.correctWork: The student swapped x and y. For (2, 5), move right 2 first (the x-coordinate), then up 5 (the y-coordinate), and place the dot at (2, 5). Plotting at (5, 2) is a different spot.
hints: In an ordered pair (x, y), the first number is always horizontal and the second is always vertical.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Graph on the Coordinate Plane is swapping the x- and y-coordinates when plotting a point — moving up first using the y-value, then moving right using the x-value, instead of always reading the ordered pair as (horizontal, vertical). For the point (3, 5), this mistake lands the dot at (5, 3) instead of the correct spot: right 3, then up 5. Before you submit, retrace your steps and check that you moved right/left using the FIRST number and up/down using the SECOND number.

exitTicket.stem: Point P is located 6 units right and 3 units up from the origin. What ordered pair names point P?
exitTicket.explanation: Right 6 = x-coordinate of 6, Up 3 = y-coordinate of 3. The ordered pair is (6, 3).
choiceFeedback: You swapped them — the x-coordinate (right) comes first.
The point moved up 3 too — the y-coordinate isn't zero.
It moved right 6 first — the x-coordinate isn't zero.
hints: Point P's moves: 6 right, then 3 up. In an ordered pair the horizontal move is written first.
Build the pair as (x, y) = (right distance, up distance). Match each number to its move before choosing.
Right 6 means the x-coordinate is 6, so the pair starts with 6. Now place the 'up 3' move in its slot.

questions.stem: A data set is symmetric. What is likely true about the mean and median?
choices: The mean is much higher than the median
The median is much higher than the mean
They are always exactly the same
questions.explanation: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are approximately equal because the data is balanced on both sides.

questions.stem: A histogram of basketball players' ages shows: most players are 22–28, with a long tail of older players up to age 40. What is the shape of this distribution?
questions.explanation: Most data is on the left (younger ages) with a tail stretching right (older ages). This is skewed right.

questions.stem: Which word describes the direction of the TAIL, not the peak?
choices: Skew — the direction of the long tail tells you the skew direction
Skew — the direction of the peak tells you the skew direction
Skew — the direction the median points
Skew — the direction of the mode
questions.explanation: The skew direction is named after the TAIL. If the tail stretches to the right, it is skewed right, even though the peak is on the left.
